list.listitem: The main goal of preconception care is to provide health promotion, screening, and interventions for women of reproductive age to reduce risk factors that might affect future pregnancies. C
Family planning is an essential part of preconception care and allows for health promotion and preventive care prior to pregnancy. C
Advise women of reproductive age to take a folic acid supplement to reduce the risks of neural tube defects. A
Pediatric visits are a great place to promote the use of folate and vitamins when mothers bring children for preventive and sick visits. B
Control of chronic diseases is essential to optimizing pregnancy outcomes. C
Update immunizations as needed for women who are planning on becoming pregnant. C

Preconception care (PCC) is defined as a set of interventions aimed at identifying and modifying biomedical, behavioral, and social risks to a woman's health or pregnancy outcome through prevention and management. It is not a single visit, but rather all health encounters during a woman's reproductive years can include counseling on appropriate medical care and behavior to optimize pregnancy outcomes, if pregnancy is desired.

By the age of 25 years, approximately 50% of women in the United States have experienced at least one birth, and approximately 85% of women in the United States have given birth by the age of 45 years.
Each year, approximately 12% of children are born prematurely, 8% are born with low birth weight, and 3% have major birth defects.
While the average American views pregnancy as routine, 31% of women giving birth suffer pregnancy-related complications.

Of women who can become pregnant, 69% do not take supplemental folic acid, 31% are obese, 3% take OTCs or prescriptions that are known teratogens, 4% have preexisting medical conditions such as diabetes, 11% smoke, and 10% drink alcohol during pregnancy.
In the U.S., more than one half of pregnant women are overweight or obese and 8% of reproductive-aged women are extremely obese, greatly increasing the risk of pregnancy complications.
Men’s preconception health needs include environmental toxins, excessive alcohol consumption, smoking, lack of exercise/obesity, and the use of illicit drugs which are known to affect fertility.

Preconception education and counseling leads to improved knowledge, self-efficacy and health locus of control and risk behavior, but there is no evidence to support a reduction in adverse pregnancy outcomes. In a survey of 242 reproductive-aged women in Belgium who planned to have (more) children, most wanted information about lifestyle, environmental exposures, working conditions and medical issues.

In a randomized clinical trial (RCT) of an integrated maternal healthcare program with preconception care compared to a standard program without preconception care in Iran, the 147 women in the integrated program had reduced risk of preterm birth (OR 0.298, 95% CI 0.12-0.74), low birth weight (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.17-0.97), maternal complications (OR 0.399, 95% CI 0.24-0.66), and neonatal complications (OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.275-0.77) compared to the 218 women in the standard program.
Providers should take advantage of multiple opportunities to provide PCC by integrating screening and management into primary care as a routine anticipatory element.

Interconception care, which is defined as care provided to women beginning with childbirth until the birth of a subsequent child, is now being emphasized as an opportune time to modify risk factors. In addition, prior pregnancy history information should be considered so that relevant investigations can be provided, as needed.
All women and men should be encouraged to develop a reproductive life plan, which allows for optimization of health prior to pregnancy and appropriate use of contraception.
Information on the March of Dimes website can be recommended to women who are considering pregnancy.

list.listitem:
The following measures are supported by good evidence: Folic acid supplementation to reduce the risk of having a child with a neural tube defect, and risk of mortality from neural tube disorders. Preconception supplemental folate, especially in the highest consumption category (greater than 730 microg/d), is also associated with a lower risk of spontaneous abortion. Preconception-initiated low-dose aspirin for women with a prior pregnancy loss does NOT prevent preterm birth and is not associated with subsequent live birth or pregnancy loss. Low-dose aspirin starting after 12-weeks of gestation appears to reduce risk of preeclampsia, small for gestational age, and preterm birth.
Administration of rubella and hepatitis B vaccines for high-risk women who are nonimmune. Moderate physical activity is associated with a higher rate of pregnancy compared to that in patients with no physical activity while vigorous physical activity is associated with infertility, based on a systematic review and meta-analysis. Smoking cessation. The CDC provides information on risks of smoking during pregnancy including preterm birth, small for gestational age, and sudden infant death syndrome. Alcohol reduction. The CDC provides information on risks of alcohol use during pregnancy including its most severe form of fetal alcohol syndrome. If alcohol abuse is identified, assist into recovery for 6 months before planning conception. If unwilling to quit, assist in choosing a highly reliable form of contraception and consideration of quitting if contemplating pregnancy. Control of diabetes mellitus prior to conception; a meta-analysis of cohort studies found a reduction in congenital malformation (NNT = 17; 95% CI, 14-24), preterm delivery (NNT = 8; 95% CI, 5-23), and perinatal mortality (NNT = 32; 95% CI, 19-109) with diabetes control. Authors of a meta-analysis of 36 primarily cohort studies of preconception care also found moderate-certainty evidence of a reduced risk of congenital malformations, perinatal mortality, preterm birth, small for gestational age, and admission to neonatal ICU. In the single RCT of 180 women with diabetes, those randomized to intensive glycemic control had a reduced rate of congenital malformations (1/135 pregnancies vs. 8/135 pregnancies) but similar rates of spontaneous abortion or perinatal death. Authors of a Cochrane review, however, found insufficient trial data to assess the effects of preconception care for women with diabetes on health outcomes for mothers and their infants.

outlines other important elements of screening, assessment, immunization, and counseling in PCC. All are based on expert opinion. C Guidelines for preconception care are available from the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ACOG) and the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada.

The following information should be obtained: Reproductive History: Prior pregnancies and outcomes - relevant investigations may be required for conditions such as prior birth defects, history of recurrent pregnancy loss or specific genetic/placental risk (e.g., thalassemia, sickle cell, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes). Cochrane authors, however, found no RCTs of preconception genetic risk assessment for thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis and Tay-Sachs disease. Family History: Screen for personal or family history of genetic disorders and refer for counseling and testing as appropriate. Online tools are available for obtaining a three-generation pedigree (e.g., www.progenygenetics.com/online-pedigree/. Accessed January 2021) Infectious Disease: Screen and treat high-risk women for chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and tuberculosis; consider hepatitis B screening in high-risk women. Screen all women for HIV based on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Guideline. Immunization: Consider rubella and varicella susceptibility. Screen and immunize women against hepatitis B, influenza, tetanus, diptheria, pertussis, measles, mumps, rubella, and COVID-19. The CDC notes that pregnant women may be more prone to serious illness from COVID-19 based on observational studies. Medications: Discontinue teratogenic medications. For women with chronic diseases, switch to safer medications and lower doses, if possible. Substance Abuse: Screen for alcohol and tobacco use, and counsel and refer as needed. Women who experience preconception stressful events smoke and drink more during pregnancy than women not exposed to these events. Mental illness: Screen for depression and anxiety, and counsel and treat as needed. A preconception history of mental health problems is strongly associated with perinatal depressive symptoms (adjusted odds ratio 8.36; 95% CI, 3.34-20.87). In addition, in a population database study, poor preconception mental health was associated with increased odds of experiencing any pregnancy complication (AOR 1.40, 95% CI 1.02-1.92) and having a low-birthweight baby (AOR 1.99, 95% CI 1.00-3.98). The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening adults for depression in clinical practices that have systems in place to assure accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and followup. B Psychosocial: Screen for domestic violence, and counsel and refer as needed. The USPSTF recommends that clinicians screen women of childbearing age for intimate partner violence and provide or refer women who screen positive to intervention services. B Toxin Exposure: Assess for household and workplace toxins. Counsel patients on limiting fish containing mercury. Fish advisories are available for national parks through the National Park Service and through local public health departments. Weight Status: All women with BMI >26 should be counseled about the risk to their own health and the risks to pregnancy. Maternal obesity carries risks of fetal macrosomia and stillbirth; the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada recommend preconception evaluation for conditions of the cardiac, pulmonary, renal, endocrine, and skin systems, as well as obstructive sleep apnea. Diet, exercise, and a structured weight-loss program should be recommended.
Even among normal weight women, pre-pregnancy diet likely influences pregnancy outcomes. For example, in a systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies with 30,871 pregnant women, healthier diets such as Mediterranean Diet, Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet and Alternate Healthy Eating Index diet (AHEI) were associated with 15% to 38% reduced relative risk of gestational diabetes (GDM) while frequent consumption of potato, meat/processed meats, and protein derived from animal sources was associated with an increased risk of GDM. In addition, engaging in >90 min/week of leisure time physical activity before pregnancy was associated with 46% decreased relative. odds of GDM. Nutrient Intake: Assess for nutritional adequacy and recommend a multivitamin if unable to meet recommended daily allowance. Advise folic acid supplement to ensure 0.4 mg (400 micrograms) daily. Recommended dose for a woman who has had a prior child with an NTD is 4000 micrograms daily.

Control Chronic Medical Conditions: Diabetes: Counsel women about the importance of diabetes mellitus control, with the goal of a near-normal HgbA1c prior to conception. Unfortunately, there are no limited data available to assess the effects of preconception care for women with diabetes on health outcomes for mothers or infants. Hypertension: Educate regarding the risks of hypertension during pregnancy and modify medication regimen (e.g., discontinue ACE inhibitors). Seizure Disorders: Counsel regarding the increased risks of seizures during pregnancy. If possible, initiate monotherapy at the lowest effective dose. Asthma: Optimize asthma control with medications prior to conception. With poor control, use effective birth control until symptom control is achieved. Systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome: Recommended assessments include disease activity, autoantibody profile, previous vascular and pregnancy morbidity, hypertension and the use of drugs, with emphasis on benefits from hydroxychloroquine and antiplatelets/anticoagulants. In addition to the items in , providers are encouraged to advocate for public and private health insurance coverage for women to improve access to preventive women's health and PCC.

Initial comprehensive preventive medicine evaluation and management of an individual including age and gender appropriate history, examination, counseling/anticipatory/risk reduction interventions and ordering of appropriate immunizations, laboratory/diagnostic procedures:

tr.td: Folic acid (400 mcg daily) for all women capable of conceiving before conception and through first trimester; 4 mg is recommended for women who have delivered a child with an open neural tube defect
Intensive preconception glycemic control in women with diabetes prevents congenital abnormalities
Women with epilepsy should be changed to monotherapy with the least toxic agent and placed on folate 1 to 4 mg/d preconception
Smoking cessation should be advised preconception because this decreases neonatal mortality and morbidity

feature.feature_body:
Recommendation References
Assess the patient's risk of chromosomal or genetic disorders based on personal and family history, ethnic background, and age; offer Cystic Fibrosis, Tay-Sachs, and other carrier screening as indicated
Screen for depression, anxiety, domestic violence, illicit drug use, and major psycho-social stressors
Screen and counsel as appropriate for smoking cessation and controlling alcohol binge or frequent drinking before conception
Assess and/or counsel the patient about possible toxins and exposure to teratogenic agents (e.g., heavy metals, solvents, pesticides, allergens) at home, in the neighborhood, and at work; review Material Safety Data and consult a local teratology specialist as needed
Assess and/or counsel the patient about oral anticoagulant, antiepileptic, Accutane, and any other high-risk medications to avoid conception, and eliminate or change to a less harmful therapy before conception
Assess the patient's body habitus (ie, BMI), clinical, and dietary risks. Encourage reaching a healthy weight before conception to reduce risks of neural tube defects, preterm delivery, diabetes, cesarean-section, and hypertensive and thromboembolic disease associated with obesity and pregnancy
Screen for periodontal, gynecologic, and STI infections as indicated
Update immunization with hepatitis B, rubella, varicella, Tdap, HPV, and influenza vaccines as needed
Laboratory testing should include a CBC; urinalysis; blood type and screen; screening for rubella, syphilis, hepatitis B, human immunodeficiency virus, gonorrhea, chlamydia, and diabetes; cervical cytology should be obtained as indicated
Promote family planning based on the patient's reproductive life plan; for those who are not planning to become pregnant, promote effective contraceptive use and discuss emergency contraception.
Promote healthy behaviors such as good nutrition, exercise, safe sex, dental flossing, and use of preventive health services; discourage risky behaviors such as douching, not wearing a seatbelt, and substance abuse
Address ongoing stressors (eg, finances, education, domestic violence) and identify resources to help the patient develop problem-solving and conflict-resolution skills, positive mental health, and strong relationships
Note: These recommendations are based on Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry recommendations and emerging practice models and, therefore, receive C ratings.Abbreviations: BMI, body mass index; STI, sexually transmitted infection; Tdap, tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis; HPV, human papilloma virus.
